events.name: The payroll run
rumor: the {ship} carries the camps' payroll out of {port} {when}. A strongbox with {cash} in it, and two clerks to sit on it.
there's a payroll going out of {port} {when} in the {ship}: {cash} for the mines, and nobody aboard but her crew and a clerk.

events.name: The storm-bound fleet
rumor: every pier in {port} is full: the gale's kept the fleet in, the warehouses are stacked to the rafters, and the crews are drinking the town dry.
half the lake's lying at {port} till the blow's done. Holds full, crews ashore, and nobody minding the sheds.

paper.headline: Fleet Storm-Bound at {port}
paper.deck: Every Berth Taken as the Gale Holds; Warehouses Full
paper.body: Steamers, tugs and schooners crowd the piers at {port} while the storm signal flies. The wharfingers report the sheds full of freight waiting on fair weather, and the saloons doing a trade not seen since the Fourth.

scene.title: A lifeboat adrift
scene.body: Your lookout sings out: a ship's boat, low in the water, four men in her and one of them waving a shirt on an oar. Their schooner opened up in the night and went down under them. They have a little money between them and nothing else.

choices.label: Take them aboard
choices.result: You bring them aboard, give them blankets and coffee, and set them ashore at the next town. They'll tell everybody who picked them up.

outcomes.text: Picked up four men from a lifeboat adrift and set them ashore.

choices.label: Take their money and leave them
choices.result: You take their purses at the rail and bear away. They'll be picked up, or they won't, and either way they'll talk.

outcomes.text: Robbed four castaways in a lifeboat and left them adrift.

choices.label: Sail on
choices.result: You stand on and the boat drops astern. Somebody else's business.

scene.title: Idle hands on the pier
scene.body: A crew sits on the stringpiece with their feet over the water, passing round an empty bottle. Their captain's gone up to the hotel for the night and left them nothing to do and nothing to drink. One of them looks at you hopefully.

choices.label: Stand them a round
choices.result: You send a boy up to the saloon with two dollars. By dark the whole crew are there, and the men on watch tonight won't need much persuading.

choices.label: Walk on
choices.result: You nod to them and walk on up the pier.

letter.subject: Provisions wanted
letter.body: Captain {captain}, — The camps are going in early this year and every pound of pork and flour at {port} is bought up already. We pay over the odds for provisions landed there this week, and the boys up the shore at Two Harbors would pay the same for whiskey, if a man had any. — J. Larsen

paper.headline: Mill Burned at {port}
paper.deck: Night Fire Takes Saw Mill and Yard; Lumber Short
paper.body: A fire that began in the engine house at {port} took the mill and most of the piled lumber in its yard before morning. Dealers say sawn lumber will be dear there until the mill is rebuilt.

events.name: A herring run
rumor: the herring are in thick off {port}: the tugs can't lift the nets, and fish are going for next to nothing on the dock. Carry them to Duluth and you'd do well.

paper.headline: Herring Run at {port}
paper.deck: Nets Too Full to Lift; Fish Cheap on the Docks
paper.body: The fall run of herring has come in thick off {port}, and the packing houses cannot salt them fast enough. Fresh fish are to be had on the docks there at prices not seen in years.

events.name: A moon-cussing night
rumor: the {ship} is due past {mark} {when}, laden to her marks. The glass is falling and there's no moon. A night for moon-cussers, the old men say, if there were any left.
no moon tonight and weather coming. They say the {ship} will be feeling her way past {mark} after dark, and her master steers by the lights and nothing else.

paper.headline: Coal Short at the Head of the Lakes
paper.deck: Colliers Late; Docks at {port} and Superior Nearly Bare
paper.body: With the colliers from Buffalo held up below and winter coming, the coal docks at {port} and Superior are near bare. Dealers ask double, and householders are told to look to their woodpiles.

paper.headline: Revenue Cutter Ordered to {region}
paper.deck: The Morrill to Patrol Against Lawlessness on the Water
paper.body: On complaints from shippers, the revenue cutter Morrill has been ordered to patrol {region} until further notice. Her commander is said to have orders to stop and search any vessel answering the description of the craft lately complained of.

letter.subject: Somebody is talking
letter.body: Captain, — A man who drinks at the Pier saloon has been asking after you, and says he knows where you keep your goods ({hideout}). He means to sell it to the marshal. He'll keep his mouth shut for {cost}, sent care of the harbor master. — A friend

choices.label: Pay him off
choices.result: You leave the money with the harbor master in a plain envelope. Nobody comes asking.

outcomes.text: Paid an informant to keep quiet.

choices.label: Let him talk
choices.result: You burn the letter. A week later the talk in the saloons is all about your hideout, and the law has heard it too.

outcomes.text: An informant sold word of your hideout to the law.

events.name: Freeze-up
rumor: {port}'s frozen in. The last boats went down the lake a week back, and the ones that didn't are laid up at the coal dock till spring.
that's the season done at {port}: ice from the piers out past the light, and the crews paid off. Fuel and flour'll be dear by February.

paper.headline: Navigation Closed at {port}
paper.deck: Ice Takes the Harbor; Vessels Laid Up for the Winter
paper.body: The ice has closed {port} to navigation for the season. The last of the fleet has cleared or gone into winter quarters, the tugs are hauled out, and the harbor master has struck his flag. Dealers report stocks of coal, flour and provisions laid in, but warn that prices will rise with the winter.

events.name: Ice-out
rumor: the ice is going out of {port}: floes all down the shore and open water at the piers. First boat in will get the town's welcome and a price for anything she carries.
{port}'s open again. Watch for floes off the points a week or two yet, they'll stave a plank.

paper.headline: The Ice Goes Out at {port}
paper.deck: Harbor Open; Watch Kept for the First Boat of the Season
paper.body: The ice went out of {port} this week before a fresh southwest wind, and the harbor is open to navigation. Floe ice still runs along the shore and off the points. The wharves are being made ready, and the town is watching the lake for the first boat of the season, whose captain will be given the customary silk hat.

events.name: The ice road marked
rumor: the ice road's marked to La Pointe: boughs every few rods from the end of the city dock, and the mail sled went over this morning.
they've tested the channel ice and staked the road across to La Pointe. Eight inches and better all the way, so a man can walk it, or haul a sled.

paper.headline: Ice Road to La Pointe Opened
paper.deck: Channel Ice Tested and the Way Marked with Evergreens
paper.body: The ice in the channel between {port} and La Pointe has been tested and found sound, eight inches and upward the whole way across, and the road has been marked with evergreen boughs from the foot of the city dock. The mail goes over by sled, and foot travel and light hauling are expected to begin at once. Travelers are cautioned to keep to the marked way.

events.name: The ice road closed
rumor: nobody's crossing to La Pointe now. The ice in the channel has gone rotten and they've pulled up the boughs.
the ice road's done for the season. You'd go through out in the middle; wait for a boat.

paper.headline: Ice Road to La Pointe Closed
paper.deck: Channel Ice Unsafe; Markers Taken Up
paper.body: The ice road between {port} and La Pointe is closed. The channel ice has gone soft and honeycombed, the evergreen markers have been taken up, and the public is warned against crossing on foot or by sled until the ice is out and the boats are running.

events.name: The Mataafa storm
rumor: the worst blow anybody's seen: the Mataafa went onto the north pier at the canal with her crew aboard, and they froze in the after cabin with the whole town on the beach watching.
a northeaster out of nowhere, eighty mile an hour down the length of the lake. Two dozen boats ashore or gone from here to the Soo.

paper.headline: STORM OF THE CENTURY
paper.deck: The Mataafa Ashore at the Ship Canal; Her Crew Lost Within Sight of the City
paper.body: A northeast gale of unexampled fury swept the head of the lakes on Monday and Tuesday. The steel steamer Mataafa, turning back for shelter, struck the north pier at the ship canal and broke in two; nine of her crew froze to death in her stern within a few hundred yards of the thousands gathered on the shore. Vessels are reported ashore from Two Harbors to the Apostles, and the loss to shipping is beyond reckoning.

events.name: Hollister undercuts you

outcomes.text: Hollister Fish & Packing cut the price they pay me for fish at {port}.

letter.from: E. T. Hollister, Hollister Fish & Packing Co.
letter.subject: Your fish
letter.body: Captain {captain}, — It has come to my notice that you have been landing fish on our dock at {port} as though you were one of the Company's own boats. You are not. From this week our buyers will give you sixty cents on the dollar for anything you bring in, and you may take it or carry it elsewhere. The Company's tugs have fished these grounds for twenty years and mean to fish them twenty more. — E. T. Hollister

rumor: Hollister's put the word out on Captain {captain}: sixty cents on the dollar for that captain's fish, and the buyers on the {port} dock are to hold to it.
old Hollister doesn't like a boat he doesn't own selling fish on his dock. Captain {captain} is getting sixty cents on the dollar, and that's him being kind.

events.name: Hollister turns your catch away

outcomes.text: Hollister's buyers at {port} will take no more of my fish.

rumor: the buyers at {port} have orders: not a pound of Captain {captain}'s fish, at any price. Hollister means to starve that captain off the grounds.

paper.headline: Packer Shuts Its Dock to {captain}
paper.deck: Hollister Buyers to Take No Fish from the Independent Captain
paper.body: The Hollister Fish & Packing Company has instructed its buyers at {port} to take no fish from {who}, who has lately been selling on the Company's dock. Mr. Hollister told this paper that the grounds are fished by the Company's tugs and that he sees no reason to buy from a man who means to take them over.

events.name: Hollister posts a reward
rumor: Hollister's offering a hundred dollars to anyone who'll tell the marshal who's been at his sheds and his tugs. He's got a fair idea already.

paper.headline: Hollister Offers $100 Reward
paper.deck: Packer's Sheds and Tugs Attacked; Company Appeals to the Law
paper.body: The Hollister Fish & Packing Company offers one hundred dollars for information leading to the arrest of the persons responsible for the damage done to its property at {port} and on the water. The marshal has been asked to look into it, and Mr. Hollister makes no secret of whom he suspects.

letter.from: E. T. Hollister, Hollister Fish & Packing Co.
letter.subject: Terms
letter.body: Captain {captain}, — This has gone on long enough, and it costs us both. The Company will buy your fish again at {port}, at eighty-five cents on the dollar, for as long as you care to sell it, on condition that it ends here. Write your answer care of the harbor master. — E. T. Hollister

choices.label: Take his terms
choices.result: You write that you accept. His buyers will take your fish again, at his price, and the Company will hear no more from you.

choices.label: Tear it up
choices.result: You tear the letter in half and leave it with the harbor master to send back. Let him find out what it costs.

events.name: You come to terms with Hollister

outcomes.text: Came to terms with Hollister Fish & Packing: their price, and the feud's done.

rumor: Captain {captain} took Hollister's terms in the end. Eighty-five cents on the dollar, and glad of it.

paper.headline: Hollister and {captain} Settle
paper.deck: Independent Captain Accepts the Company's Price
paper.body: The quarrel between the Hollister Fish & Packing Company and {who} is at an end. The captain has accepted the Company's terms and will sell at {port} at its price. Mr. Hollister said he was pleased that good sense had prevailed.

events.name: Hollister gives (the sheds)

outcomes.text: Hollister Fish & Packing gave in: their sheds had cost them more than my fish ever would.

letter.from: E. T. Hollister, Hollister Fish & Packing Co.
letter.subject: Enough
letter.body: Captain {captain}, — I cannot prove what I know, and I have stopped trying. Our buyers at {port} will take your fish again, and pay you the best price on the dock and a little over. I ask only that the Company's sheds be left alone. — E. T. Hollister

rumor: Hollister's given up. Two nights' brine spoiled and his warehouse cleaned out, and now he pays Captain {captain} over the odds for fish just to be let alone.

paper.headline: Hollister Gives Way
paper.deck: Packer Reopens Its Dock to {captain} After a Season of Trouble at Its Sheds
paper.body: After a season in which its packing house and warehouse at {port} were repeatedly broken into and its stock spoiled, the Hollister Fish & Packing Company has made its peace with {who}, whose fish it lately refused. Nothing has been proved, and Mr. Hollister would say only that the Company wished to put the matter behind it.

events.name: Hollister gives (the tugs)

outcomes.text: Hollister Fish & Packing gave in: they couldn't keep their tugs on the grounds with me about.

letter.from: E. T. Hollister, Hollister Fish & Packing Co.
letter.subject: Enough
letter.body: Captain {captain}, — My tug captains will not go out while your sail is on the lake, and I cannot blame them. Our buyers at {port} will take your fish again at the best price on the dock and a little over. Leave the Company's boats alone. — E. T. Hollister

rumor: Hollister's tugs are lying in the slip with their nets dry. Their skippers won't go out while Captain {captain} is about, and the old man's paying that captain over the odds to keep the peace.

paper.headline: Fish Tugs Stay in Port
paper.deck: Hollister Makes Peace with {captain} After Its Boats Are Robbed
paper.body: The Hollister Fish & Packing Company, several of whose tugs have been stopped and robbed on the grounds this season, has reopened its dock at {port} to {who} and will pay the captain's price. The Company's skippers say they will not fish while the matter stands, and Mr. Hollister has evidently decided that it shall not.

events.name: Hollister gives (out-traded)

outcomes.text: Hollister Fish & Packing gave in: I'd out-traded them, and {port} knew it.

letter.from: E. T. Hollister, Hollister Fish & Packing Co.
letter.subject: A proposal
letter.body: Captain {captain}, — You have made your point. The fish you will not sell us has gone to Duluth and Superior at a better price, and the town has taken your side. Our buyers at {port} will take your fish again at the best price on the dock and a little over, if you will bring it to us first. — E. T. Hollister

rumor: Captain {captain} beat Hollister fair and square: carried the catch to Duluth and made friends of half of {port} doing it. Now the old man's paying over the odds to get that fish back.

paper.headline: Independent Beats the Packer
paper.deck: {captain} Wins Hollister's Custom After the Company Shut Its Dock
paper.body: When the Hollister Fish & Packing Company closed its dock at {port} to {who}, the captain carried the catch down the lake instead and sold it there. The Company has now reopened its dock to the captain, at a price above its own boats', and the town is said to be well pleased. It is a good season for the independent fisherman.

events.name: Poker night
rumor: there's a big game at the card table in {port} tonight. The captains are putting up more than money: a cargo, or a contract, or a map. Come with a full purse.

paper.headline: High Stakes at {port}
paper.deck: Captains Wager Whole Cargoes Across the Card Table
paper.body: It is said along the waterfront at {port} that a card game in one of the saloons is being played for whole cargoes, and that more than one master has gone back to his vessel lighter than he came ashore. The constable is said to take no notice.

events.name: The papers give you a name

letter.subject: {nick}
letter.body: Captain {captain}, — Our readers have taken a lively interest in your doings, and this paper has taken the liberty of giving you the name by which the lake will know you: {nick}. Should the name displease you, our columns are open to a letter from you, which we will print in full on the fourth page. We do not undertake to print a second. — The Editor

choices.label: Write to the editor
choices.result: Your letter runs on the fourth page under the heading “A Correction.” The editor prints it in full, and the next week the papers have another name for you: {nick}.

outcomes.text: Wrote to the editor about the name the papers gave me.

choices.label: Let it stand
choices.result: You let it stand. There are worse things to be called on the waterfront.

letter.from: H. L. Dahl, Land Agent and Notary Public, Bayfield
letter.subject: Coming ashore
letter.body: Captain {captain}, — It is said along the waterfront that you have done well for yourself, {wealth} or near it, and that the law has no particular quarrel with you at present. A captain so placed might think of coming ashore while the going is good. I have three properties on my books that would suit: forty acres and a house at Peshtigo, cleared and fenced; a saloon with a good bar and rooms over it on St. Croix Avenue, Duluth; and a fisherman's cabin with a dock and a net house on Sand Island. Any one of them for cash, and no questions asked as to where the cash came from. Write me care of the harbor master. — H. L. Dahl

choices.label: Buy the farm at Peshtigo
choices.result: You write Mr. Dahl that you'll take the farm, and pay him in gold.

choices.label: Buy the saloon in Duluth
choices.result: You write Mr. Dahl that you'll take the saloon, and pay him in gold.

choices.label: Buy the cabin on Sand Island
choices.result: You write Mr. Dahl that you'll take the cabin, and pay him in gold.

choices.label: Not yet
choices.result: You put the letter in your coat. The lake isn't done with you yet.

letter.from: J. C. Merriam, United States Marshal, Western District of Wisconsin
letter.subject: A proposal
letter.body: Captain {captain}, — I will be plain. There is nobody on the south shore who knows the islands, and the ways of the people who work them, honestly or otherwise, as you do, and the Government has a use for that knowledge. The district wants a deputy on the lake. The pay is a deputy's fees and mileage; the badge comes with it, and so does a clean slate so far as this office is concerned. I am told you have friends in the ports and no warrant out against you worth the paper. That is rare enough in your line that I mean to take advantage of it. Reply care of the harbor master. — J. C. Merriam

choices.label: Pin on the badge
choices.result: You write the marshal that you accept, and take the train for Superior to be sworn.

choices.label: Decline the honor
choices.result: You write the marshal a polite refusal. He will ask again, his kind always does.

events.name: A copycat takes to the lake

outcomes.text: The talk is of a new pirate in {region}: {rival}, in {rivalShip}. One who {method}, they say, as I do.

paper.headline: A NEW PIRATE ON THE LAKE
paper.deck: {Rival} Takes Up the Black Trade in {Region}
paper.body: Not content with one freebooter, the lake has bred another. Masters in {region} report a schooner, {rivalShip}, under one {rival}, who {method}. Old hands say he has read every line printed about Captain {captain} and means to outdo it.

rumor: there's a new one out in {region}: {rival}, sailing {rivalShip}. He {method}, same as the one in the papers.
{nick}, they're calling him. Lies up somewhere out by {camp}, so the fishermen say, and hunts the boats in {region}.

events.name: A copycat strikes your lane

paper.headline: {NICK} AGAIN
paper.deck: The Pirate {Rival} Strikes in {Region}
paper.body: The schooner {rivalShip} was seen again this week in {region}, where {rival} {method}. Whether the lake has one pirate or two, the masters who ply it are past caring.

rumor: {nick}'s been at it again in {region}. Some say it was him; some say it was the other one.
you hear about {region}? {rivalShip} again. {Nick} {method}, bold as you like.

letter.subject: A word between us
letter.body: Captain {captain}, — There is not water enough on this lake for the two of us to go on as we are, crossing each other's wakes and taking each other's blame. I have a proposal. Come to the saloon at {parleyPort} and we will talk it over like men of business. I will be there this week and no longer. — {nick}

choices.label: Go and hear him out
choices.result: You'll meet {nick} in the saloon at {parleyPort}.

choices.label: Burn the letter
choices.result: You burned it. Let him find his own water.

events.name: A parley in the saloon: a truce

scene.title: {Rival} at the corner table
scene.body: He's where he said he'd be, at the back of the saloon with his hat on the table and a glass he hasn't touched. 'Here's my offer,' says {nick}. 'You don't work like me and I don't work like you. When the crews tell their tale, there's no mistaking which of us it was, and neither hangs for the other's work.' He holds out his hand.

choices.label: Shake on it
choices.result: You shook. {Nick} finished his glass in one and was gone out the back.

choices.label: Send the boy for the constable
choices.result: The constable came by the front as {nick} went out the back. But the law has his name now, and his haunts.

choices.label: Turn him down
choices.result: 'Suit yourself,' says {nick}, and goes.

events.name: A parley in the saloon: a split

scene.title: {Rival} at the corner table
scene.body: He's waiting at the back of the saloon, a chart of the lake spread out under the lamp. 'Too many of us on too few lanes,' says {nick}. 'I'll take my business elsewhere and leave {region} to you. We stay out of each other's water, and there's prizes enough for both.' He holds out his hand.

choices.label: Shake on it
choices.result: You shook. {Nick} rolled up his chart and said you'd not see his topsails in {region} again.

choices.label: Send the boy for the constable
choices.result: The constable came by the front as {nick} went out the back. But the law has his name now, and his haunts.

choices.label: Turn him down
choices.result: 'Then we'll see who's left in the spring,' says {nick}, and goes.

outcomes.text: {rival} broke our bargain and sold my name to the law.

letter.subject: Our bargain
letter.body: Captain {captain}, — You'll have noticed the law is closer behind you this week. I thought it only fair to tell you it was me. A man must look after his own. — {nick}

paper.headline: PIRATE TURNS INFORMER
paper.deck: {Rival} Said to Have Sold a Rival to the Law
paper.body: The authorities in {region} acknowledge a tip from an unlikely quarter: the pirate {rival}, it is said, has given up the haunts of Captain {captain}. There is no honor among thieves on Lake Superior either.

events.name: A copycat is caught

paper.headline: PIRATE TAKEN
paper.deck: {Rival} in Irons; {RivalShip} Seized
paper.body: The law in {region} has taken the pirate {rival}, whose schooner {rivalShip} was surprised at anchor off {camp}. He is to be tried at the next term and is expected to hang. The masters of {region} breathe easier; the papers wonder aloud who is next.

rumor: they've got {nick}. Surprised him at anchor off {camp}, they say. He'll hang.
one less pirate on the lake: {rival}'s in irons.

events.name: A copycat is lost in a gale

paper.headline: PIRATE SCHOONER LOST
paper.deck: {RivalShip} Believed Gone Down With All Hands
paper.body: Wreckage found on the shore of {region} after the gale is said to be that of {rivalShip}, the schooner of the pirate {rival}. The lake, it seems, has done what the law could not.

rumor: {rivalShip} went down in the blow, they say. {Nick} and all his crew.
the lake took {nick}. Wreckage all along the beach.

events.name: A copycat gives it up
rumor: {nick}'s given it up, they say. Sold {rivalShip} and gone west with what he had.
no more {nick}. The trade's not what it was, he said, and took the train to the Dakotas.

outcomes.text: Beat {rival} and took {rivalShip}. His crew talked: he keeps his stash {campWhere}.

paper.headline: PIRATE AGAINST PIRATE
paper.deck: {Rival} Beaten on the Open Lake by Captain {captain}
paper.body: In an affair the like of which these waters have not seen, the pirate {rival} and his schooner {rivalShip} were run down in {region} by none other than Captain {captain}. Who is to be thanked and who hanged, the authorities have not said.
